analysis.one_liner: Bars offshore oil and gas leasing near coastal states that have banned such drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or vote: it sat in a House subcommittee from March 1999 until the Congress ended, despite 32 cosponsors including two Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act so the Interior Secretary could not sell new offshore oil and gas leases in federal waters next to any coastal state whose governor or legislature has put a moratorium on drilling. In other words, if a state has said no to offshore drilling along its own shores, the federal government could not lease the waters just beyond for drilling either. It never received a committee hearing or a vote in either chamber.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, and vacation on the coasts of states with drilling moratoria, especially in California and other states that have opposed offshore drilling. Blocking new leases near their shores lowers the risk of oil spills that can close beaches, damage fisheries, and hurt tourism. The bill gave states' own drilling bans force over the adjacent federal waters, where leasing decisions are normally made in Washington.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Coastal residents, fishing and tourism communities

how_it_helps.text: It would prohibit the Interior Secretary from issuing any new lease for mineral exploration, development, or production on Outer Continental Shelf lands that are seaward of or adjacent to a coastal state with a moratorium on oil, gas, or other mineral activities, as established by state statute or by order of the governor [S2][S3].

This would give a state's own decision to ban offshore drilling control over the federal waters directly off its coast, rather than leaving those leasing decisions entirely to the federal government [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas companies would lose access to potential new leases in federal waters off states with drilling bans, forgoing exploration and production revenue there. The federal government would forgo any lease sale revenue and royalties those waters might have produced, and the nation would forgo some potential domestic energy supply.

drawbacks.text: The bill would let a single governor block federal mineral leasing in adjacent federal waters, which critics of state veto power over federal resources consider an overreach, since those waters and their royalties belong to the nation as a whole [S3].

Restricting leasing in waters adjacent to moratorium states would reduce the area available for domestic offshore oil and gas development, cutting potential federal royalty revenue and domestic energy supply [S2].

Federal moratoria on much offshore drilling already existed administratively during this period, so the bill's practical gain was to lock that protection into statute rather than depend on each president's decision, a benefit that would only matter if a future administration tried to lift the ban.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people on moratorium-state coastlines, protection from new nearby drilling has real value: spills can close beaches and fisheries for years, and coastal tourism and fishing support many local jobs. The cost is forgone potential domestic energy production and federal royalties in those waters, which the oil industry and energy-supply advocates would point to. The bill was simple and narrow, but it never got far enough for Congress to weigh these trade-offs in the open.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Lois Capps introduced the Coastal States Protection Act on March 9, 1999, joined by 32 cosponsors — 30 Democrats and 2 Republicans [S1][S4].

The House referred it to the Committee on Resources on the day it was introduced, and on March 16, 1999 it was sent to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, with executive comment requested from the Interior Department [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the 106th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests are better off because the bill died: no statutory bar was created on leasing in federal waters next to drilling-moratorium states, leaving leasing decisions to the administration of the day.

for.name: Rep. Lois Capps
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and organized 32 cosponsors, most of them California Democrats

for.name: Rep. George Miller of California
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor when the bill was introduced

against.name: House Natural Resources Committee leadership
against.role: The committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or committee vote; the bill sat in its Energy and Mineral Resources subcommittee until the Congress ended

against.name: Rep. Don Young
against.what_they_did: Chaired the committee that received the bill and never advanced it to a hearing or vote; Alaska's congressional leadership has generally opposed offshore drilling restrictions

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic — 30 of 32 cosponsors were Democrats, with 2 Republicans — and the bill never advanced in a House controlled by Republicans.

industries.note: The bill would have removed potential new lease sites in federal waters adjacent to moratorium states, cutting off exploration and production opportunities there. Those companies profit from drilling in coastal waters, where spills impose costs on beaches, fisheries, and coastal towns.
Blocking new drilling leases near moratorium-state coasts reduces oil-spill risk that can close beaches and disrupt fisheries. These industries depend on clean coastal waters for their livelihoods.
